Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

vignette: Thomas, a 55-year-old counselor from a small Midwestern town, was twelve hours into a night-time workshop when the building's sprinkler system failed to activate. A burst pipe sent a torrent of water down the hallway, but a loose vent in the ceiling gave way, allowing a hot plume of smoke to surge through the stairwell. The acrid smell of burnt insulation was followed by a shattering sound as a stack of bookshelves collapsed onto the corridor floor. Glass shattered, fragments splintering across the carpet, and a neighbor's baseball bat was hurled across the room, striking the glass and sending shards scattering. Thomas was frozen for a moment, heart pounding as the scent of smoke filled his lungs, the sudden violence of the thrown objects rattling his nerves. Years later, that particular scent-burnt plastic and charred wood-has become a trigger that instantly transports him back to that chaotic night. The memory of the smoke's hot taste and the sharp crack of glass now underlies every intrusive flash of the event, illustrating how the sensory triggers of the original scene directly feed into his recollections. The same night left Thomas with a new, debilitating routine. The memory of objects hurled at him and the smell of smoke made the idea of any gathering in his own home-or even a simple coffee meeting with colleagues-feel like stepping into a potential flashpoint. He began to decline invitations from old friends, preferring to stay in his apartment and monitor his breathing, fearing that the slightest change might signal danger. When a co-worker mentioned a weekend retreat, Thomas thought only of the sprinkler failure, of how the sound of distant banging in the hallway had felt like a prelude to violence. His avoidance of social contact and the avoidance of even thinking about the night became a way of preempting the panic that the triggers could provoke. In this way, the sensory triggers directly influence Thomas's maladaptive strategies of avoidance. Thomas's own internal narrative-"my body is still fighting for my safety" and "I must always be on guard"-has shaped how he interprets the echoes of that night. The conviction that his heart would race again with a single whiff of burnt plastic or a crackling noise has made him hyper-vigilant. When he hears the faint hiss of a radiator in his own home, he immediately believes it could be a sign that the building is in danger. These constant appraisals of threat, rooted in the belief that his body remains in a state of defense, have heightened his sense of danger and have reinforced the vividness of the memory, demonstrating how negative appraisals can feed back into the recollection of the event. When Thomas relives the night in his mind, he feels a peculiar sense of alienation; the images feel foreign, as though someone else endured them. The dissonance between his body's physical reactions-tachycardia, sweating-and the narrative that he is still in danger deepens the emotional charge of the memory. The alien feeling is intensified by his belief that his own body is an enemy, always preparing for attack. The memory's emotional intensity, in turn, sharpens his sense that every small noise could be a harbinger of disaster, underscoring how the memory itself heightens his negative appraisals. The intrusive images of smoke and the crack of thrown objects do not stay confined to his mind; they bleed into his senses. Whenever Thomas passes by a construction site or walks past a bakery, the faint scent of smoke can trigger a visceral recall of the night. The sensory echo of that memory, coupled with his belief that his body will always be on guard, brings a sharp, sudden dread, illustrating how the memory actively triggers the very sensations that originally set the trauma in motion. Thomas's avoidance of friends and his constant monitoring of his thoughts have paradoxically preserved the memory's salience. By refusing to engage with the social context that might offer reassurance, he keeps the memory alive, revisiting it each time he avoids a potential threat. His vigilant thought monitoring-checking himself for any signs of mental breakdown-keeps him on the edge, ensuring that the memory remains fresh and that his negative appraisals persist. The cycle is self-reinforcing: his avoidance keeps the memory present, which in turn reinforces his beliefs that he must stay vigilant and avoid thinking about the event. Years after the building's collapse, Thomas finds himself increasingly isolated, both socially and professionally. He often skips community counseling sessions because the idea of being in a group evokes the sound of a distant clatter, a reminder of that night's chaos. The fear that any small spark could ignite another disaster keeps him from fully engaging with clients who seek help for their own anxieties. The weight of his own fear has made it difficult for him to see the possibility of healing, and the constant loop of triggers, memory, and appraisals has left him feeling trapped in the past. Now, after a recent session in which he openly expressed how the memory feels like it belongs to someone else and how his body reacts as if danger is imminent, Thomas has finally decided to seek therapy, hoping to break the cycle and reclaim a sense of safety and connection.
